questions.question: Which statement best distinguishes the L1 norm from the L2 norm when used to measure quantization error in a vector of weights?
questions.choice_A: L1 measures the sum of absolute errors, making it more robust to outliers than L2, which squares errors and emphasizes large deviations.
questions.choice_B: L1 squares the errors while L2 sums absolute errors, so L1 is more sensitive to large deviations.
questions.choice_C: Both L1 and L2 emphasize outliers equally, but L1 is easier to compute.
questions.choice_D: L2 norm equals the maximum error, whereas L1 equals the mean error.

questions.question: In the context of scaling heuristics for symmetric uniform quantization, what is a key motivation for using RMS (root-mean-square) scaling over max-based scaling?
questions.choice_A: RMS scaling completely eliminates clipping for any distribution.
questions.choice_B: RMS scaling minimizes the mean absolute error for all distributions.
questions.choice_C: RMS scaling is less sensitive to rare outliers, leading to a step size that better matches the bulk of the distribution.
questions.choice_D: RMS scaling produces a bias-free quantizer regardless of the rounding rule.

questions.question: Which property of unbiased stochastic rounding is most relevant for reducing systematic drift in accumulated sums during low-precision training?
questions.choice_A: It ensures the quantized value always rounds toward zero.
questions.choice_B: It makes the expected rounding error zero conditioned on the input.
questions.choice_C: It minimizes the worst-case absolute error compared to deterministic rounding.
questions.choice_D: It eliminates the need for clipping by expanding the dynamic range.

questions.question: For a uniform mid-tread quantizer with step size $\Delta$ and no clipping, which classical result is used to approximate quantization noise variance under the white-noise model?
questions.choice_A: $\Delta^2 / 6$
questions.choice_C: $\Delta / 2$
questions.choice_D: $\Delta^2$

questions.question: Which scenario is most likely to invalidate the white-noise model assumption for quantization error?
questions.choice_A: Inputs are i.i.d., zero-mean Gaussian with small variance relative to the step size.
questions.choice_B: The quantizer is high resolution and the input distribution is smooth.
questions.choice_C: The input is strongly correlated with the quantization grid, leading to signal-dependent errors.
questions.choice_D: Dither is added before quantization to decorrelate the error.

questions.question: What is the primary trade-off when choosing max-based scaling for weights in a layer?
questions.choice_A: Reduced clipping at the cost of larger step size and increased rounding noise for most values.
questions.choice_B: Increased clipping at the cost of smaller step size and decreased rounding noise.
questions.choice_C: Improved bias properties but worse variance properties.
questions.choice_D: Lower latency but higher dynamic power.

questions.question: Which statement about clipping is correct in the context of quantization error?
questions.choice_A: Clipping reduces variance but may introduce bias by saturating tails of the distribution.
questions.choice_B: Clipping always reduces both bias and variance of quantization error.
questions.choice_C: Clipping has no effect on bias if deterministic rounding is used.
questions.choice_D: Clipping only affects positive values and not negative values.

questions.question: When comparing per-layer versus per-channel scaling for convolutional weights, which advantage is most commonly associated with per-channel scaling?
questions.choice_A: Per-channel scaling reduces the number of scaling parameters and improves generalization.
questions.choice_B: Per-channel scaling better matches the dynamic range of each output channel, typically reducing quantization error.
questions.choice_C: Per-channel scaling eliminates the need for calibration data.
questions.choice_D: Per-channel scaling guarantees unbiased quantization noise.

questions.question: Which measure is most appropriate when the goal is to control the worst-case quantization error over a tensor?
questions.choice_A: Mean absolute value
questions.choice_B: L2 norm
questions.choice_C: L1 norm
questions.choice_D: Max (infinity) norm

questions.question: Which phenomenon explains why quantization can increase the variance of activations even if the expected error is zero?
questions.choice_A: Bias amplification
questions.choice_B: Error heteroscedasticity due to signal dependence of step size
questions.choice_C: Additive white noise added by rounding increases the second moment
questions.choice_D: Vanishing gradients in deep networks

questions.question: Suppose we use mean-absolute (L1-based) scaling to set the step size. Which distributional property makes this heuristic particularly appealing compared to RMS scaling?
questions.choice_A: It is optimal in the maximum-likelihood sense for Gaussian data.
questions.choice_B: It is less sensitive to heavy tails and outliers than RMS scaling.
questions.choice_C: It guarantees no clipping for any symmetric distribution.
questions.choice_D: It minimizes the Kullback–Leibler divergence to the unquantized distribution.

questions.question: Under what condition is the quantization error approximately uncorrelated with the signal in uniform quantization?
questions.choice_A: When the quantizer step size is large relative to the signal variability
questions.choice_B: When dithering is used or when the input spans many quantization intervals with smooth density
questions.choice_C: When deterministic round-to-zero is used
questions.choice_D: When clipping is severe

questions.question: Which rounding rule can reduce bias introduced by systematic truncation in accumulators during low-precision training?
questions.choice_A: Round-toward-zero
questions.choice_B: Round-away-from-zero
questions.choice_C: Banker's rounding (round-to-nearest, ties to even)
questions.choice_D: Floor function

questions.question: In analyzing error propagation across layers, why is the layer’s Lipschitz constant relevant?
questions.choice_A: It determines whether the layer preserves unbiasedness of noise.
questions.choice_B: It bounds how much input perturbations (including quantization noise) can be amplified by the layer.
questions.choice_C: It indicates whether the layer is invertible under quantization.
questions.choice_D: It ensures the noise is Gaussian after the layer.

questions.question: Consider a symmetric $b$-bit uniform quantizer with scale $s$ mapping real value $x$ to integer $q \in \{-(2^{b-1}-1), \dots, 2^{b-1}-1\}$. Which factor primarily controls the trade-off between rounding noise and clipping?
questions.choice_A: The choice of integer bit-width $b$ alone
questions.choice_B: The choice of stochastic vs deterministic rounding alone
questions.choice_C: The choice of scale $s$ that maps the real dynamic range to the representable integer range
questions.choice_D: The sign of $x$

questions.question: Why can per-channel activation quantization be harder than per-channel weight quantization in deployed inference systems?
questions.choice_A: Activations change per input example, complicating the use of distinct runtime scales per channel.
questions.choice_B: Weights are statistically nonstationary, while activations are stationary.
questions.choice_C: Per-channel scaling increases model size only for activations.
questions.choice_D: Per-channel activation quantization prevents vectorization on any hardware.

questions.question: Which statement best characterizes the bias–variance trade-off in quantization when adjusting clipping thresholds?
questions.choice_A: Lower thresholds reduce bias but increase variance.
questions.choice_B: Higher thresholds reduce variance but can increase bias by rounding more values.
questions.choice_C: Lower thresholds increase bias from saturation but reduce variance by lowering step size.
questions.choice_D: The trade-off only exists for stochastic rounding, not deterministic rounding.

questions.question: In the white-noise model, how does quantization noise propagate through a linear layer with weight matrix $W$?
questions.choice_A: The output noise covariance is $W W^\top$ regardless of input noise.
questions.choice_B: The output noise variance scales with the squared singular values of $W$, i.e., covariance transforms as $W \Sigma W^\top$.
questions.choice_C: Noise remains unchanged since linear layers preserve variance.
questions.choice_D: Noise becomes zero if $W$ is orthogonal.

questions.question: What is a practical role of calibration data in post-training quantization (PTQ)?
questions.choice_A: It guarantees training-free optimization of the network weights.
questions.choice_B: It determines per-layer or per-channel scales and clipping thresholds that balance rounding noise and saturation on representative inputs.
questions.choice_C: It eliminates the need for rounding by learning exact integer representations.
questions.choice_D: It proves that the white-noise model holds for the network.

questions.question: Which intervention most directly aims to decorrelate quantization error from the signal so that the white-noise model is a better approximation?
questions.choice_A: Using larger batch sizes during training
questions.choice_B: Adding subtractive dither before quantization
questions.choice_C: Using ReLU activations
questions.choice_D: Switching to max-based scaling

questions.question: When comparing MSE (mean squared error) and MAE (mean absolute error) as objectives for choosing a quantization scale, which is generally true?
questions.choice_A: MSE penalizes large errors more heavily, often favoring scales that fit the bulk at the expense of outliers.
questions.choice_B: MAE penalizes large errors more heavily than MSE, making it less robust to outliers.
questions.choice_C: MSE and MAE yield identical optimal scales for any symmetric distribution.
questions.choice_D: MAE scales are always preferred for Gaussian data because they minimize variance.
